with_sayso.order-retry: A timeout means the wait ended with no response, so you do not know whether the order was placed. A second attempt can place a second order. Retry only if the request carries an idempotency key the server will honor, or after you confirm this order is not already there. A connection reset means the other side aborted the TCP connection. If that happens before the server receives the request — during connect, or on a reused connection while the request is still going out — the order was not placed, and you can retry. If it happens after the request was fully sent, the server may already have placed the order, so confirm that it does not exist before you retry.

with_sayso.load-note-review:
`load_note` returns whatever file `open` reads, and it stores that text in `cache` under `name` alone. Three problems change what a caller gets.

The path is not confined to that user's notes. `user_id` and `name` go into the path with no check. `open` resolves `..`, so a `..` segment in either value makes this call return a file outside `/notes/{user_id}/`. A `user_id` of `""` or `"."` collapses the path to `/notes/{name}`, so the caller receives that file instead of a file inside a user directory. The opened text is what gets stored at `cache[name]`. Reject a `user_id` that is empty, `.`, `..`, or contains a separator, so it can only be a single directory name. Then open the note only when its resolved path is still inside `/notes/{user_id}`.

The bytes are decoded with the process locale. `open(path)` passes no encoding, so the returned string depends on the locale. The same file can decode to different text under another locale. Bytes that locale cannot decode raise `UnicodeDecodeError`, and the caller gets that exception. Pass the encoding the notes use. If the files are UTF-8, the call is `open(path, encoding="utf-8")`. The snippet does not record that encoding.

The cache entry ignores `user_id`. `cache[name] = text` keeps a single value per name. After `load_note("alice", "todo")` and then `load_note("bob", "todo")`, `cache["todo"]` holds bob's text, so a later read of `cache["todo"]` returns bob's note. Each call still returns the file it just read. Store the text at `cache[(user_id, name)]`.

Overlapping calls are left open. The read and the cache assignment are separate steps, and the function does not serialize them. A second caller can observe the previous `cache[name]` only if something else can run in that gap and read `cache`. The snippet does not show that caller.

with_sayso.hash-lookup:
People call hash map lookup O(1) because, with keys spread evenly and the load factor kept bounded, the expected search stays constant as the map grows. The hash selects a bucket directly. Under that even spread, the expected lookup is proportional to 1 plus the load factor, the number of entries divided by the number of buckets. As the map grows it resizes, which keeps the load factor bounded and the expected lookup constant.

A weak hash, or keys chosen to collide, can put every entry in one bucket. In a chain or a probe sequence, the lookup then walks the whole map, and the worst case is linear in the number of entries. If the load factor grows with the map, the average bucket gets longer, and the expected lookup grows with it. With open addressing, where a collision probes other slots, the expected number of probes climbs sharply as the table gets close to full. The O(1) label treats hashing and comparing the key as constant work. A very long key makes one lookup proportional to the size of the key.

An insert that rebuilds the table copies every entry, so that insert is linear in the size of the map. Over a sequence of inserts those rebuilds average out, which is the amortized O(1) claim for insertion. A lookup runs against the buckets already there, so its cost is that bucket walk.

without_sayso.load-note-review:
Path interpolation treats `user_id` and `name` as raw path segments. A value containing `/` or `..` makes `open` read a different file (another user’s note, or a path outside `/notes`). The caller gets that file’s contents, or `FileNotFoundError` / `IsADirectoryError` when the resolved path is missing or a directory.

The cache is stored under `name` only. Loads of the same name for different users leave a single `cache[name]` entry, holding whichever write finished last, so a later cache read returns the other user’s text. Every `load_note` call returns the string just read from disk.

`open(path).read()` decodes with the process locale encoding and turns newlines into `\n`. The returned string changes with the locale, and bytes that encoding cannot decode raise `UnicodeDecodeError`.

The file object is never closed. After enough calls the process runs out of descriptors, and later callers get `OSError`.

without_sayso.hash-lookup:
Hash map lookup is called O(1) because a hash function turns the key into a bucket index in one shot, and—when keys are spread out and the table stays a constant fraction full—that bucket holds only a small, bounded number of entries. Finding the key is then a fixed amount of work no matter how many items are stored. That bound is an average (expected) cost under a decent hash and a capped load factor, and inserts stay O(1) only in the amortized sense because an occasional resize walks the whole table.

The description stops holding when collisions pile up. A weak hash, or keys chosen to land in the same bucket, makes one chain (or one probe sequence) grow with the number of entries, so lookup becomes O(n) in the worst case. It also slips when the load factor is left unbounded and chains keep lengthening, when you count a single resize instead of amortizing it, and when the key itself is large: hashing and comparing a string or blob costs time proportional to the key’s length, which the O(1) shorthand treats as free.
